items.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Jim Robinson wasn’t considered as no great trombone player. They was as old as Kid Ory. They ain’t never went nowhere.

ctx.x: How did he sound? There’s not much . . . George Boyd never recorded.

No. They all had that sound of bending notes, playing the blues and all, but they all played in tune. They never deviated from playing some other notes or bending a note wrong. They played within the context of the music. That’s what’s got to be watched when you’re playing a clarinet. You got to play that [expletive deleted] in tune, because it reflects. You got a problem on a note, [? (inaudible)] if you know it, but you got to play that clarinet in tune. If you play like George Lewis, he was never considered a…

items.title: 52115_Danny Barker oral history interview
items.q: Jim Robinson was a trombone player who became...supposed to have been the greatest New Orleans trombone player after Kid Ory.

ctx.x: You mentioned Jim Robinson, a trombonist. Who was he?

Jim Robinson was a trombone player who became...supposed to have been the greatest New Orleans trombone player after Kid Ory. Now, he was in that band. He was probably out to ...(?)... that band. But the Australian trombone players, they all got something from Jim Robinson -- which is the same pattern he plays in every chorus. [SINGS TWO BAR REFRAIN] He played the bass trombone.
